title: The soul at peace
hook: O soul at peace, return: said at death, or on the Day of Judgment?
tomorrow: what would it be like to see the One you've prayed to?

segments.voice: Yesterday: my last words. La ilaha illallah, rehearsed over a life, prompted gently at the end. Today, the words said back to the soul.
screen: `MY LAST WORDS.` → `NOW, THE WORDS SAID BACK.`

segments.voice: Some voice notes get replayed just for the tone: someone you love saying your name like they're glad you exist. The Qur'an has a call like that near the end of the surah called the Dawn, in Pickthall's words: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure! Enter thou among My bondmen! Enter thou My Garden!" So who is being called, and when? Muslim commentators have answered that in more than one way.
screen: `A VOICE NOTE, REPLAYED.` → `BUT AH! THOU SOUL AT PEACE!` → `WHO, AND WHEN?`

segments.voice: The soul at peace is al-nafs al-mutma'innah: the self that has settled, that rests in Allah instead of running. Not a soul that never struggled; a soul that came to rest. Now the debate about the moment. One view: these words are said at death. Some early commentators reported that the angels speak them to the believer's soul as it leaves. At its best, this view puts a gentle welcome at the hardest door. The other view: they're said on the Day of Judgment. The verses just before describe that Day, the earth ground down and the angels in ranks, so the call comes as the answer to all of it: enter among My servants, enter My Garden. At its best, this view keeps the verses in their place in the surah. Some commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, mention both. And both views share the heart of it. The Arabic pairs two words: radiyah, pleased, and mardiyyah, pleasing. The soul is pleased with its Lord, and its Lord is pleased with it. One small detail: in these verses, the soul isn't sent anywhere. It's invited back.
screen: `A SELF THAT HAS SETTLED.` · `VIEW ONE: SAID AT DEATH.` · `VIEW TWO: SAID ON THAT DAY.` · `PLEASED, AND PLEASING.` · then, large: `RETURN, PLEASED.`

segments.voice: Find the quietest sound around you: a fan, a fridge's hum, your own breath. Rest your attention on it, the way a settled soul rests instead of running. When your mind runs off, come back to the sound.
screen: `THE QUIETEST SOUND.` · `REST ON IT.` · `COME BACK WHEN YOU WANDER.`

segments.voice: The soul at peace: the self that has settled in Allah, called home in the Qur'an, pleased with its Lord and pleasing to Him.
The call to carry: return, pleased, and welcomed home as pleasing to Him. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1774 COUNTS.` → `THE JOURNEY HOME · 9 OF 11.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WOULD IT BE LIKE TO SEE HIM?`

howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah al-Fajr's closing verses (89:27–30) in prayer and sometimes at funerals and graves; commentators differ on whether the call comes at death or on the Day of Judgment, and some hold both.

fork.setup: your dad says 89:27 is spoken on the Day of Judgment. your grandmother says it's said at death, and you agree with her. what's your dad's best case?
options: the verses come right after the passage about that Day, as its answer.
death is too sad a moment for words this hopeful.

fork.reveal: at its best, the Judgment-Day reading keeps the call in its place in the surah: the answer to the Day just described. the at-death reading's best case: a welcome at the hardest door.

what a scholar hears: Qur'an 89:27-30, radiyatan mardiyyah; reports of the angels saying it at death beside the Judgment-Day reading from context (89:21-26); Ibn Kathir records both.

chat.says: imam recited 'O soul at peace' at Friday prayer. Dadi says it's about dying. Dad says Judgment Day. who's right?
options: Both are real readings; some commentators give both. Either way the soul returns pleased, and pleasing.
Dadi. The commentators all agree it's what the angels say at the very moment of death.
Dad. The Qur'an doesn't speak about the moment of death at all, only about the Last Day.
chat.meaning: Commentators differ on when 89:27–30 is said: at death, or on the Day of Judgment; Ibn Kathir mentions both. Both share the welcome: pleased and pleasing.
